ProblemSolutionFeaturesArchitectureWalkthroughChallengesOutcomeTeamFuture

The problem

Make everyday travel more shareable when traffic, cost, and rigid transport options create friction.

The project presentation frames the problem around heavy urban traffic, pollution, inconsistent public-transport schedules, and the cost of individual travel. It explores carpooling as a way to connect people travelling in compatible directions while making better use of existing vehicles.

The solution

Organize shared rides around clear driver, passenger, and administrator workflows.

WEE RIDE was developed as a web-based carpooling system with three primary roles. Drivers manage trip information and incoming ride requests, users search for available trips and request seats, and administrators monitor the system and manage application data.

Register→Search or offer ride→Request→Driver review→Ride history→Admin oversight

The supplied project material demonstrates the main account, ride, request, and administration flows.

Driver screens show trip/account details, booking requests from users, and a request-management view for reviewing ride participation.

03

User / client workflow

User screens demonstrate searching available trips, opening ride details, requesting rides, and reviewing past rides.

04

Administration

The administrator interface includes a dashboard, monitoring/control screens, and data-management views for the application's operational records.

System architecture

Use a browser-based UI with the PHP/MySQL application stack documented in the project presentation.

The original web-application diagram identifies HTML, CSS, Bootstrap and AngularJS on the interface side, PHP and MySQL in the application/data stack, XAMPP with Apache/MySQL for the local environment, and HTTP POST/GET with JSON responses between browser and server. Engineering challenges

Coordinate multiple roles and ride states without turning research ideas into claimed implementation.

The source material does not document a bug-by-bug development diary, so these are the engineering challenges visible in the demonstrated system rather than invented incident stories.

01 · Multi-role workflow design

Drivers, passengers, and administrators need different screens and actions while still operating on the same ride and booking information.

02 · Ride and request state

The user journey spans ride discovery, a booking request, driver review, status updates, and ride history, which requires consistent state across several views.

03 · Frontend-backend-data flow

The project architecture connects browser interfaces to PHP/MySQL through HTTP requests, so forms, request handling, and stored records need to agree on the same data flow.

Results & key learnings

A working academic demonstration of role-based carpooling workflows.

01

Account workflow

The project demonstrates registration and role-specific login entry points.

02

Ride discovery and requests

User screens show available trips and ride-request workflows, while driver screens show incoming booking requests and request management.

03

Administrative visibility

The dashboard and data-management interfaces demonstrate system-wide oversight of operational records.

The project provided practical exposure to full-stack workflow design, role-oriented interfaces, form/data handling, browser-to-server communication, relational data, and turning an application idea into a demonstrable multi-screen system. The supplied material does not establish production deployment, scale, performance benchmarks, or commercial usage.

Team context

Present the work accurately as a collaborative academic project.

The project presentation credits three student team members, including Asmita G V. It does not document a reliable breakdown of individual implementation responsibilities, so this case study does not assign sole authorship or invent personal contribution claims.

Future improvements

Extend the platform beyond the demonstrated web workflows.

The presentation lists multilingual support, integration with campus events, enhanced security measures, and integration with public transportation as future directions. These are presented here as proposed improvements, not completed features.
